lessons.theory:
## Introduction

An Operating System (OS) is system software that manages computer hardware and software resources, and provides common services for computer programs. It acts as an intermediary between users and hardware, managing CPU, memory, storage, and I/O devices. Examples include Windows, Linux, macOS, and Android.
## Key Concepts

- Operating System: A program that manages hardware and provides services to applications
- Kernel: The core of the OS — runs in privileged mode, manages CPU, memory, I/O
- System Call: Interface between user programs and the kernel (open(), read(), write(), fork())
- User Mode vs Kernel Mode: User mode = restricted access, Kernel mode = full access
- Batch OS: Jobs processed in batches, no user interaction
- Time-Sharing OS: Multiple users share CPU time (multitasking)
- Real-Time OS: Strict timing constraints (RTLinux, VxWorks)
- Distributed OS: Multiple computers work as one system

## Important Formulas

- `CPU Utilization = (Busy Time / Total Time) × 100%`
- `Throughput = Number of processes completed per unit time`
- `Turnaround Time = Completion Time - Arrival Time`
- `Waiting Time = Turnaround Time - Burst Time`
- `Response Time = First CPU allocation - Arrival Time`

## Comparison Tables

| OS Type | Characteristic | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Batch | Jobs processed sequentially, no interaction | Early IBM mainframes |
| Time-Sharing | Multiple users, quick response | Unix, Linux |
| Real-Time | Guaranteed response time | VxWorks, RTLinux |
| Distributed | Multiple networked computers | Amoeba, LOCUS |
| Mobile | Touch interface, power management | Android, iOS |


## Summary

An Operating System (OS) is system software that manages computer hardware and software resources, and provides common services for computer programs. It acts as an intermediary between users and hardware, managing CPU, memory, storage, and I/O devices. Examples include Windows, Linux, macOS, and Android.

analogies.mapping: Customers = processes, Waiters = system calls, Kitchen = CPU, Tables = memory. The manager (OS) schedules which customer gets served next, allocates tables, and resolves disputes.
Guests = processes, Rooms = memory frames, Receptionist = memory manager. Fixed partitioning = rooms of one size; paging = uniform room blocks; virtual memory = overbooking.

lessons.title: Process Management and Scheduling
lessons.overview: A process is a program in execution. Process management involves creating, scheduling, suspending, and terminating processes. The OS uses scheduling algorithms to decide which process gets the CPU and for how long. Key concepts include process states, the PCB (Process Control Block), context switching, and various CPU scheduling algorithms.
keyConcepts: Process: A program in execution (active entity, has PCB)
Program: A set of instructions on disk (passive entity)
PCB (Process Control Block): Data structure storing process info (PID, state, PC, registers, memory info)
Process States: New → Ready → Running → Waiting → Terminated
Context Switch: Saving the state of one process and loading another
Preemptive Scheduling: OS can force a running process to give up CPU
Non-Preemptive Scheduling: Process keeps CPU until it finishes or blocks
FCFS: First Come First Serve — simple but may cause convoy effect
SJF: Shortest Job First — optimal but needs future knowledge
Round Robin: Each process gets a time quantum, then preempted
Priority Scheduling: Highest priority process runs first
formulas: FCFS: Avg Waiting Time = (Σ Waiting Time) / n
SJF (non-preemptive): Sort by burst time, then schedule
Round Robin: Time Quantum = q; if burst > q, preempt and add to ready queue
Turnaround Time = Completion Time - Arrival Time
Waiting Time = Turnaround Time - Burst Time
commonMistakes: Forgetting to sort by arrival time before applying FCFS
In SJF, choosing the shortest remaining time at each preemption point (SRTF is preemptive SJF)
In Round Robin, not adding the preempted process to the END of the queue
Confusing waiting time with response time
examTips: Draw the Gantt chart for each scheduling algorithm
Calculate: Completion Time → Turnaround Time → Waiting Time → Average
For Round Robin, show the ready queue at each time quantum
For SJF, always pick the shortest burst among arrived processes

lessons.theory:
## Introduction

A process is a program in execution. Process management involves creating, scheduling, suspending, and terminating processes. The OS uses scheduling algorithms to decide which process gets the CPU and for how long. Key concepts include process states, the PCB (Process Control Block), context switching, and various CPU scheduling algorithms.
## Key Concepts

- Process: A program in execution (active entity, has PCB)
- Program: A set of instructions on disk (passive entity)
- PCB (Process Control Block): Data structure storing process info (PID, state, PC, registers, memory info)
- Process States: New → Ready → Running → Waiting → Terminated
- Context Switch: Saving the state of one process and loading another
- Preemptive Scheduling: OS can force a running process to give up CPU
- Non-Preemptive Scheduling: Process keeps CPU until it finishes or blocks
- FCFS: First Come First Serve — simple but may cause convoy effect
- SJF: Shortest Job First — optimal but needs future knowledge
- Round Robin: Each process gets a time quantum, then preempted
- Priority Scheduling: Highest priority process runs first

## Important Formulas

- `FCFS: Avg Waiting Time = (Σ Waiting Time) / n`
- `SJF (non-preemptive): Sort by burst time, then schedule`
- `Round Robin: Time Quantum = q; if burst > q, preempt and add to ready queue`
- `Turnaround Time = Completion Time - Arrival Time`
- `Waiting Time = Turnaround Time - Burst Time`

## Comparison Tables

| Algorithm | Type | Pros | Cons |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| FCFS | Non-preemptive | Simple, fair | Convoy effect, poor avg wait |
| SJF | Non-preemptive | Optimal avg wait | Starvation for long jobs |
| Round Robin | Preemptive | Fair, good response time | High context switch overhead |
| Priority | Both | Important jobs first | Starvation (solve with aging) |


## Code Examples

### Example

```c
// Process Control Block structure
struct PCB {
  int pid;            // Process ID
  int state;          // NEW, READY, RUNNING, WAITING, TERMINATED
  int program_counter; // Next instruction address
  int registers[16];   // CPU registers
  int priority;        // Scheduling priority
  int burst_time;      // CPU time needed
  int arrival_time;    // When process arrived
  struct PCB *next;    // Next PCB in ready queue
};
```

## Summary

A process is a program in execution. Process management involves creating, scheduling, suspending, and terminating processes. The OS uses scheduling algorithms to decide which process gets the CPU and for how long. Key concepts include process states, the PCB (Process Control Block), context switching, and various CPU scheduling algorithms.

lessons.title: Memory Management and Paging
lessons.overview: Memory management is the process of controlling and coordinating computer memory, assigning portions called blocks to various running programs, and optimizing system performance. Key concepts include contiguous allocation, paging, segmentation, and virtual memory. Paging eliminates external fragmentation by dividing memory into fixed-size frames.
keyConcepts: Logical Address: Address generated by the CPU (virtual address)
Physical Address: Address in RAM (actual address)
MMU (Memory Management Unit): Hardware that maps logical to physical addresses
Contiguous Allocation: Each process gets a single contiguous block of memory
Fragmentation: External (free space between allocated blocks) and Internal (wasted space within a block)
Paging: Divide logical memory into pages and physical memory into frames (same size)
Page Table: Maps page numbers to frame numbers
Segmentation: Memory divided into segments of variable size (based on program structure)
Virtual Memory: Uses disk as extension of RAM — enables running programs larger than RAM
Page Fault: Occurs when a referenced page is not in RAM (must be fetched from disk)
formulas: Page Number = Logical Address / Page Size
Physical Address = Frame Number × Page Size + Offset
Number of Pages = Process Size / Page Size
TLB Hit Ratio = TLB Hits / Total Accesses
commonMistakes: Forgetting that page size = frame size (they must be the same)
Confusing internal fragmentation (within allocated block) with external (between blocks)
Not computing the physical address correctly: Frame × PageSize + Offset
examTips: Always compute: Page# = Address / PageSize, Offset = Address % PageSize
Draw the page table with page number → frame number mapping
For virtual memory, explain page fault handling steps
Compare paging vs segmentation in a table

lessons.theory:
## Introduction

Memory management is the process of controlling and coordinating computer memory, assigning portions called blocks to various running programs, and optimizing system performance. Key concepts include contiguous allocation, paging, segmentation, and virtual memory. Paging eliminates external fragmentation by dividing memory into fixed-size frames.
## Key Concepts

- Logical Address: Address generated by the CPU (virtual address)
- Physical Address: Address in RAM (actual address)
- MMU (Memory Management Unit): Hardware that maps logical to physical addresses
- Contiguous Allocation: Each process gets a single contiguous block of memory
- Fragmentation: External (free space between allocated blocks) and Internal (wasted space within a block)
- Paging: Divide logical memory into pages and physical memory into frames (same size)
- Page Table: Maps page numbers to frame numbers
- Segmentation: Memory divided into segments of variable size (based on program structure)
- Virtual Memory: Uses disk as extension of RAM — enables running programs larger than RAM
- Page Fault: Occurs when a referenced page is not in RAM (must be fetched from disk)

## Important Formulas

- `Page Number = Logical Address / Page Size`
- `Offset = Logical Address % Page Size`
- `Physical Address = Frame Number × Page Size + Offset`
- `Page Size = 2^n (typically 4KB = 2^12)`
- `Number of Pages = Process Size / Page Size`
- `TLB Hit Ratio = TLB Hits / Total Accesses`

## Comparison Tables

| Concept | Paging | Segmentation |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Block Size | Fixed (page size) | Variable (segment size) |
| Fragmentation | Internal only | External only |
| Address Space | One-dimensional | Two-dimensional (segment, offset) |
| Visibility | Invisible to user | Visible to user |
| Table | Page table | Segment table |


## Summary

Memory management is the process of controlling and coordinating computer memory, assigning portions called blocks to various running programs, and optimizing system performance. Key concepts include contiguous allocation, paging, segmentation, and virtual memory. Paging eliminates external fragmentation by dividing memory into fixed-size frames.
